questions.question: How does LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) fine-tune a large model?
options: Adds new tokens to the vocabulary and trains only their embeddings
Trains all base weights, but with a very small learning rate
Prunes the layers that matter least and retrains the remaining ones
Freezes the base weights and trains small low-rank update matrices
questions.explanation: LoRA keeps W frozen and learns ΔW = B·A with a small rank r, injected into Transformer layers. Only A and B are trained, which cuts trainable parameters and optimizer memory dramatically.

source.title: Hu et al., LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models

questions.question: Which two claims about LoRA are supported by the original paper? (Select two.)
options: Once merged into the weights, it adds no extra inference latency
It can cut trainable parameters about 10,000× versus fully fine-tuning GPT-3
It always beats full fine-tuning by a wide margin on every benchmark task
It requires pre-training the model again from scratch with the adapters
It only works on image models, not on language models
questions.explanation: The paper reports about 10,000× fewer trainable parameters and 3× lower GPU memory than full fine-tuning of GPT-3 175B with Adam. B·A can be merged into W, so there is no added latency. Quality is on par with full fine-tuning, not always far better.

source.title: Hu et al., LoRA (Abstract)

questions.question: A company wants one base model in production with a different customization for each of 20 customers. Why is LoRA convenient for this? (Select two.)
options: LoRA removes the need to store the base model
One shared base model can serve and swap many adapters
LoRA merges all customers into one model automatically
LoRA trains 20 full model copies at no extra cost
Each customer needs only a small adapter file
questions.explanation: LoRA adapters are tiny (often megabytes) compared with the base model. Many customer adapters can be stored and swapped or served on one shared base, which is much cheaper than 20 fully fine-tuned copies. The base model is still needed.

source.title: Hu et al., LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models

questions.question: In LoRA, what does increasing the rank r generally do?
options: Fewer trainable parameters, so the adapter gets smaller and faster
The tokenizer gains new tokens for every extra unit of rank
The frozen base weights become trainable along with the adapter
More trainable parameters and capacity, at a higher memory cost
questions.explanation: The rank sets the inner dimension of A and B. Higher r means more trainable parameters and a more expressive update, but more memory and risk of overfitting. The paper found small ranks often work well.

source.title: Hugging Face PEFT, LoRA conceptual guide

questions.question: What does QLoRA add on top of LoRA?
options: The adapters are trained in FP64 for maximum numerical accuracy
The LoRA adapters are replaced by full fine-tuning of all weights
The frozen base is stored in 4-bit NF4; LoRA adapters train on top
Only the tokenizer and embeddings are quantized to 4-bit integers
questions.explanation: QLoRA quantizes the frozen base weights to 4-bit NormalFloat, uses double quantization and paged optimizers, and trains LoRA adapters. The paper fine-tuned a 65B model on a single 48 GB GPU with 16-bit-level task performance.

source.title: Dettmers et al., QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs

questions.question: What is the key idea of prompt tuning (soft prompts)?
options: Fine-tune all model weights, using only prompts as training data
Learn soft embedding vectors prepended to the input; weights frozen
Train a new task-specific tokenizer and keep the model frozen
Hand-write better prompts in natural language and test them
questions.explanation: Prompt tuning learns a few 'virtual token' embeddings that are prepended to the input and trained by backpropagation. They are not readable text. The base model is frozen, and the method becomes competitive with full fine-tuning as models get larger.

source.title: Lester et al., The Power of Scale for Parameter-Efficient Prompt Tuning

questions.question: According to NVIDIA's description of p-tuning, how are the virtual tokens produced?
options: A small trainable prompt encoder generates them for the task
They are copied directly from the labels of the training data
The vector database retrieves them from similar past prompts
A prompt engineer writes them by hand as natural-language text
questions.explanation: P-tuning trains a small model (prompt encoder) that outputs virtual token embeddings for the task. After tuning, the virtual tokens are stored in a lookup table and used at inference in place of the small model. The LLM itself is not retrained.

source.title: NVIDIA Blog, Prompt Engineering and P-Tuning

questions.question: Classic adapter modules (Houlsby et al.) differ from LoRA mainly because they:
options: Insert extra bottleneck layers that add some inference latency
Learn virtual tokens that are prepended to the input text
Train all of the model's weights, but in a lower precision
Modify only the tokenizer and leave the network untouched
questions.explanation: Adapters add new small feed-forward bottleneck layers between existing layers and train only those. They are parameter-efficient, but the extra layers run at inference time. LoRA's update can be merged into the weights, so it adds no latency.

source.title: Houlsby et al., Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning for NLP

questions.question: Prefix tuning differs from prompt tuning because it:
options: Uses discrete text prefixes written by human experts
Learns prefix vectors only at the input embedding layer
Trains all model weights, starting from a text prefix
Learns prefix vectors at every layer, not only at the input
questions.explanation: Prefix tuning optimizes task-specific continuous vectors that every layer's attention can attend to. Prompt tuning learns embeddings only at the input layer. Both keep the base model frozen.

source.title: Li & Liang, Prefix-Tuning: Optimizing Continuous Prompts for Generation

questions.question: After full fine-tuning on legal documents, a model performs well on legal tasks but has become much worse at general questions it used to answer well. What is this called?
options: Quantization error from the update
Catastrophic forgetting
Data leakage from the test set
Underfitting
questions.explanation: Catastrophic forgetting is the loss of previously learned capabilities when a network is trained on new data. PEFT methods, mixing in general data, lower learning rates and fewer epochs reduce it.

source.title: Hugging Face LLM Course, Fine-tune LLMs (Chapter 11)

questions.question: What does supervised fine-tuning (SFT, instruction tuning) of a pre-trained LLM use as training data?
options: Prompts paired with a scalar score from a reward model
Unlabeled web text, with the next token as the only label
Prompts or instructions paired with high-quality responses
Human rankings that compare several responses per prompt
questions.explanation: SFT trains the model on demonstrations: instruction or prompt and desired output, often in a chat template. Ranking data is used to train reward models or for preference optimization such as DPO.

source.title: Hugging Face LLM Course, Fine-tune LLMs (Chapter 11)

questions.question: A team wants a model to always answer in a specific JSON style and tone for a narrow task. Prompting works about 85% of the time. Which next step usually gives the best effort-to-gain ratio?
options: Pre-training a new model from scratch on company data
Adding RAG over the company's general documentation
LoRA fine-tuning on a few thousand curated examples
Switching to a model ten times larger, without testing
questions.explanation: Consistent format and style is a behaviour, not missing knowledge, and fine-tuning teaches behaviour well. PEFT is cheap compared with full fine-tuning or pre-training. RAG adds knowledge, not style.

source.title: Hugging Face PEFT documentation

questions.question: Which two statements correctly compare RAG and fine-tuning? (Select two.)
options: Both RAG and fine-tuning require pre-training a new model from scratch
Fine-tuning suits teaching a consistent style, format or behaviour
RAG suits knowledge that changes often: update documents, no training
Fine-tuning automatically gives a source citation for every answer it generates
RAG permanently changes the model's weights each time documents are added
questions.explanation: RAG injects up-to-date, citable knowledge at query time. Fine-tuning changes weights and is effective for behaviour and style. They are complementary and often combined. Neither needs pre-training from scratch.

source.title: NVIDIA Blog, What Is Retrieval-Augmented Generation?

questions.question: What are the three main stages of the classic RLHF pipeline?
options: Reward model → pre-training → SFT on the reward model's labels
SFT model → reward model from human rankings → RL (e.g. PPO)
Quantize the model → prune weights → distill into a student
Tokenize → embed the corpus → retrieve context → generate
questions.explanation: RLHF starts from a pretrained (often instruction-tuned) model, trains a reward model on human rankings of outputs, and then optimizes the policy with PPO against that reward, with a KL penalty to stay close to the original model.

source.title: Hugging Face Blog, Illustrating RLHF

questions.question: In RLHF, why do annotators usually rank several model outputs instead of giving each one an absolute score?
options: Rankings make the final model smaller and faster to serve
Rankings can be generated without any human involvement
Absolute scores cannot be used to train any neural network
Comparisons are more consistent across annotators than scores
questions.explanation: Different people calibrate absolute scores differently, so scores are noisy. Relative comparisons ('A is better than B') are more reliable, and the reward model learns a scalar reward from them.

source.title: Hugging Face Blog, Illustrating RLHF

questions.question: During the RL step of RLHF, what is the purpose of the KL-divergence penalty against the initial model?
options: It replaces the human preference data with the KL divergence
It keeps the policy close to the original and limits reward hacking
It pushes the policy as far as possible from the original model
It speeds up training by skipping the reward model for most steps
questions.explanation: Without a constraint, the policy can find outputs that score highly on the reward model but are gibberish (reward hacking). The KL penalty keeps outputs close to the original model's distribution.

source.title: Hugging Face Blog, Illustrating RLHF

questions.question: How does Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) differ from PPO-based RLHF? (Select two.)
options: It uses no preference data at all, only unlabeled text from the web
It only works for image generation models, not for language models
It needs three separate reward models instead of one, trained in sequence
It trains directly on preference pairs with a simple classification-style loss
It needs no separate reward model and no RL sampling loop
questions.explanation: DPO reparameterizes the RLHF objective so the optimal policy can be fit directly on (chosen, rejected) pairs. It skips training a reward model and running PPO, which makes it simpler, more stable and lighter. It still needs preference data.

source.title: Rafailov et al., Direct Preference Optimization

questions.question: What does a single training example look like for DPO?
options: A prompt with one correct target response
A raw web document with no prompt at all
A prompt with a chosen and a rejected response
A prompt with a scalar reward from 1 to 10
questions.explanation: DPO learns from preference pairs: for each prompt, one better and one worse completion, usually judged by humans or a strong model. SFT uses single target responses.

source.title: Rafailov et al., Direct Preference Optimization

questions.question: What did the InstructGPT study find about alignment with human feedback?
options: Labelers preferred a 1.3B InstructGPT over the 175B GPT-3
RLHF made outputs less helpful but much more truthful
Labelers preferred the 175B GPT-3 over every aligned model
Human feedback only worked once models exceeded 100B parameters
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning GPT-3 with SFT and RLHF made it better at following instructions. Even the 1.3B InstructGPT was preferred over the 175B base model, which shows that alignment data can matter more than scale for helpfulness.

source.title: Ouyang et al., Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback

questions.question: Constitutional AI replaces much of the human labeling in alignment by:
options: The model is trained with no safety data at all, to avoid bias
Lawyers write every training example based on a national constitution
An AI critiques outputs against written principles; AI feedback trains preferences
Keyword filters remove unsafe outputs, so no further alignment training is needed
questions.explanation: Constitutional AI uses a list of principles. The model self-critiques and revises responses in a supervised phase, then AI-generated preference labels train the preference model (RL from AI Feedback).

source.title: Bai et al., Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback

questions.question: A team is preparing a web-scraped corpus for LLM pre-training. Which two steps are standard parts of data curation? (Select two.)
options: Removing all punctuation and capital letters
Translating everything into one language without checking quality
Quality filtering with heuristics or classifiers
Deduplication (exact and near-duplicate removal)
Duplicating the best documents 100 times
questions.explanation: Curation pipelines such as NeMo Curator remove exact and fuzzy duplicates and filter low-quality, toxic or boilerplate text, along with language identification and PII handling. Heavy duplication of data harms generalization.

source.title: NeMo Curator, Key Features

questions.question: Why is deduplicating pre-training data important? (Select two.)
options: Duplicated lines make the tokenizer crash during pre-training
Deduplication increases the size of the dataset in tokens
Repeated text encourages memorization and verbatim regurgitation
Duplicates waste training compute on the same tokens
Duplicates reliably improve how well the model generalizes
questions.explanation: Repeated documents make models memorize and regurgitate text and waste training tokens. Duplicates of test data can also inflate benchmark scores. Near-duplicate detection, for example with MinHash, is a standard curation step.

source.title: NeMo Curator documentation

questions.question: A model scores surprisingly high on a public benchmark. The team then finds the benchmark questions in its training corpus. What is this problem called?
options: Mode collapse in the decoder
Catastrophic forgetting of earlier tasks
Data contamination (test-set leakage)
Gradient explosion during pre-training
questions.explanation: If evaluation data appears in training data, scores measure memorization rather than capability. Decontamination, removing n-gram overlaps with benchmarks, should be part of data preparation.

source.title: Brown et al., Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (contamination analysis)

questions.question: Before fine-tuning on customer support transcripts, what must be done about names, emails and phone numbers?
options: Nothing, because LLMs never memorize training data
Duplicate them so the model learns customers' details
Translate them so they no longer look like personal data
Detect and remove or mask the personal data (PII)
questions.explanation: LLMs can memorize and reproduce training data. PII should be redacted or pseudonymized, with a proper legal basis and consent, before training. This is both a privacy requirement and good practice.

source.title: NVIDIA, Trustworthy AI (Privacy)

questions.question: A team has only 200 labeled examples for a new classification task and uses a strong LLM to generate 5,000 more. What is the most important follow-up?
options: Use the synthetic examples as the test set for the final model
Check its quality and labels, and evaluate on real held-out data
Delete the 200 real examples so the data style is consistent
Train only on the synthetic data and skip the evaluation step
questions.explanation: Synthetic data can be repetitive, biased or mislabeled. It should be filtered and checked, and the model must be evaluated on real data the generator didn't produce. Using synthetic data as the test set hides problems.

source.title: Wang et al., Self-Instruct: Aligning Language Models with Self-Generated Instructions

questions.question: When preparing a chat fine-tuning dataset for an instruction-tuned model, why use the model's own chat template?
options: Chat templates encrypt the training data to protect user privacy
Chat templates are only needed for image-text models
The model expects its own role markers and special tokens
Chat templates shrink the vocabulary to save memory
questions.explanation: Each chat model expects a specific format (system, user and assistant markers and special tokens). Training or prompting with a different format confuses the model. Hugging Face's apply_chat_template applies the right one.

source.title: Hugging Face, Chat templates

questions.question: During fine-tuning, training loss keeps falling but validation loss starts rising after epoch 2. What should the team do?
options: Train for 20 more epochs until training loss reaches zero
Increase the learning rate tenfold to escape the minimum
Remove the validation set because it disagrees with training
Keep the best validation checkpoint and stop early
questions.explanation: Rising validation loss with falling training loss is overfitting. Keep the checkpoint with the best validation score and consider fewer epochs, more data, dropout or a lower learning rate.

source.title: Hugging Face LLM Course, Fine-tune LLMs (Chapter 11)

questions.question: Which two hyperparameters most directly influence whether LLM fine-tuning overfits or forgets? (Select two.)
options: The logging frequency of the trainer
The name of the output checkpoint folder
Learning rate
Number of training epochs
The tokenizer's vocabulary size
questions.explanation: Too high a learning rate or too many epochs push the model away from its pre-trained knowledge and overfit the small dataset. Both should be tuned against a validation set.

source.title: Hugging Face LLM Course, Fine-tune LLMs (Chapter 11)

questions.question: When annotators label data for fine-tuning or RLHF, what is the best way to check that labels are reliable?
options: Let each annotator use their own criteria to capture diversity
Use one annotator for everything, so labels stay consistent
Clear guidelines plus inter-annotator agreement on shared items
Accept all labels and let the model average out the noise
questions.explanation: Labeling quality depends on clear instructions and calibration. Measuring agreement between annotators on shared items, for example with Cohen's kappa, reveals ambiguous guidelines or unreliable labelers.

source.title: scikit-learn, cohen_kappa_score

questions.question: A team preparing data for RLHF collects pairs of model answers and asks users to choose the better one. Which RLHF component is this data used to train?
options: The tokenizer
The reward model
The embedding index
The learning-rate scheduler
questions.explanation: Human comparisons train the reward model to output a scalar preference score, and the policy is then optimized against it. The same pairs could also be used directly with DPO.

source.title: Hugging Face Blog, Illustrating RLHF

questions.question: What is the usual order of escalation when adapting an LLM to a new task, from cheapest to most expensive?
options: PEFT → pre-training → prompting → full fine-tuning
Prompting → PEFT → full fine-tuning → pre-training
Pre-training → full fine-tuning → PEFT → prompting
Full fine-tuning → prompting → pre-training → PEFT
questions.explanation: Start with the cheapest option (prompting, few-shot, RAG for knowledge). Move to parameter-efficient methods if needed, then full fine-tuning. Pre-training a model is by far the most expensive.

source.title: NVIDIA Blog, Prompt Engineering and P-Tuning

questions.question: A team fine-tunes with LoRA and uses the same learning rate as a published full fine-tuning recipe. Training barely improves. What is a common reason?
options: LoRA needs the tokenizer to be retrained first
LoRA cannot be trained with gradient descent at all
LoRA usually needs a higher learning rate than full fine-tuning
LoRA usually needs a much lower learning rate than full fine-tuning
questions.explanation: LoRA's B matrix starts at zero and only a small number of parameters are trained, so typical LoRA learning rates are higher than full fine-tuning rates. Hyperparameters must be tuned per method.

source.title: Hugging Face PEFT, LoRA conceptual guide

questions.question: When preparing a dataset with the Hugging Face datasets library, why is .map() with batched=True commonly used for tokenization?
options: It tokenizes many examples per call and caches the results
It removes the need for a tokenizer by using raw bytes
It shuffles the dataset so that batches are more balanced
It downloads a new tokenizer for every batch of examples
questions.explanation: Dataset.map(batched=True) processes batches of examples, which works well with fast (Rust) tokenizers. Results are cached on disk, so large datasets can be processed efficiently.

source.title: Hugging Face LLM Course, The Datasets library (Chapter 5)
